holding_summary: The court held that keeping an inn or tavern in the common-law sense is a lawful trade open to any citizen without a license; only the added privilege of selling spirituous liquors on the premises requires an excise license. Because the defendant's sign reading 'Entertainment' (paired with a 'Temperance' placard) did not indicate that he sold liquor, it did not amount to the statutory offense of displaying an unlicensed tavern sign.

quotes.text: But, at common law, any person may erect an inn for the public accommodation, without a license; as the keeping of it is not a franchise, but a lawful trade open to every citizen.

holding_summary: Mrs. Switzer, a married woman, hired houses in her own name and ran a boarding-house business, contracting with boarders and receiving their payments; she gave defendant a note and chattel mortgage on the boarding-house furniture. The court held that because the mortgaged furniture went into the joint possession of husband and wife and was used for the family's support, it was not the wife's separate property under the Acts of 1848-49, so the husband alone was liable for its price and the wife's note and mortgage could not be enforced.

quotes.text: there was no separate property of the wife, the husband was liable for the debts contracted by the wife for its payment; consequently the note and mortgage given by the wife for its payment could not be enforced.

notes: Court's holding turns on married women's property/coverture law, not on the legal character (lease/license/lodging) of the boarding arrangement itself, so characterization and polarity are left null.

holding_summary: An indictment will lie against excise commissioners who wilfully and corruptly grant a tavern license to an applicant they know is not of good moral character, lacks sufficient ability to keep a tavern, lacks the necessary accommodations for travellers, or where a tavern is not actually necessary at that place, notwithstanding the commissioners' ordinary discretion in licensing decisions.

quotes.text: that he is of sufficient ability to keep a tavern ; and has the necessary accommodations to entertain travellers; and that a tavern is absolutely necessary for the actual accommodation of travellers at the place where such applicant resides or proposes to keep the same

By demurring, the defendants concede that they granted the license in question to a person whom they knew was not a mail of good moral character, nor a man of sufficient ability to keep a tavern; that he had not the necessary accommodations, and that a tavern was not necessary at the place where he proposed to keep it. This was a clear violation of duty, for which they were liable to be indicted.

holding_summary: The court enjoined the city of Brooklyn from enforcing, against a licensed innkeeper, a municipal ordinance that banned all liquor sales on Sunday, because state excise law expressly permitted licensed innkeepers to sell to their lodgers and lawful travelers on Sunday; the ordinance was therefore void as applied to the plaintiff's licensed privilege of serving his lodgers.

quotes.text: An ordinance, passed by a municipal corporation prohibiting the sale of spiritous liquors on Sunday, is void so far as relates to sales by innkeepers, to . their lodgers and to lawful travelers, pursuant to their licenses, and an injunction will be granted, to prevent its enforcement against them.
